records.sourceTitle: The Reptile Database, Varanus mabitang, Gaulke & Curio 2001

facts.value: A Panay Island endemic described from northwest Panay. Published records should not be extended automatically to other Visayan islands.

The Reptile Database quotes the original comparison with Varanus olivaceus. Mabitang has a dark dorsal surface dotted with small yellow marks, unlike the contrasting grey-green pattern described for Gray's monitor.
The species belongs to the Philippine monitor group often discussed under Varanus (Philippinosaurus).

records.caution: An arboreal monitor photo needs close comparison, viewing angle and locality evidence. Coloration alone is not a validated identification.

records.sourceTitle: The Reptile Database, Varanus bitatawa, Welton et al. 2010

facts.value: The Sierra Madre forest monitor is a Philippine species described from the northeastern Luzon area.
The original description cited a large, robust body and contrasting black and yellow dorsal pattern, with other scalation and anatomical characters distinguishing it from Varanus olivaceus.
The Reptile Database indicates that the species is largely fruit-eating in published accounts.

records.caution: Photographed large arboreal lizards need specialist comparison. Keep non-invasive observations and do not identify from fruit feeding alone.

facts.value: The Reptile Database lists Cebu, Ticao, Negros, Panay and Masbate for the species; exact local evidence needs source verification.
The database describes noticeably enlarged raised nuchal scales on the neck as a central characteristic.
Earlier names placed the species under Varanus salvator, which can cause confusion in old literature.

records.caution: Do not infer occurrence from the historical name 'water monitor' or reuse a Varanus salvator identification without review.

records.sourceTitle: The Reptile Database, Cuora philippinensis, Blanck et al. 2023

facts.value: The Philippine box turtle was separated from older Cuora amboinensis concepts in the 2023 published taxonomy used by the database.
The account lists multiple Philippine islands, including the Visayas, Luzon and Mindanao; occurrence records under the older complex require reconciliation.
Species identification should rely on the original taxonomic diagnosis rather than the general presence of a hinged turtle shell.

records.caution: Past observations labeled Cuora amboinensis are not silently reidentified as Cuora philippinensis.

facts.value: A Philippine forest turtle with historical combinations under Heosemys. It is not interchangeable with the black marsh turtle Siebenrockiella crassicollis.
The original type was reported from southern Leyte, but the taxonomic account discusses Palawan and a complicated collection history. The name is not proof of current occurrence on Leyte.
The database describes freshwater river and swamp habitats.

records.caution: Use verified contemporary records when describing actual island range; a historically reported type locality must be distinguished from verified present-day distribution.

facts.value: The Asian giant softshell turtle has a broad Asian distribution, with Philippines among the cited countries.
Described as inhabiting freshwater rivers and tributaries, with occasional entry into brackish waters.
Historic names under Pelochelys bibroni or Pelochelys cantoris can require reconciliation with modern taxonomy.

records.caution: Distinguish exact taxon and geographic records from other softshell turtles. Do not infer breeding or feeding from an isolated photograph.

facts.value: This pit viper is documented from Batan Island in the Batanes group, not across the entire Philippine archipelago.
The species has been listed under Trimeresurus flavomaculatus mcgregori in older literature and later reinstated as a species.
The source cites a fully arboreal habit in comparative viper ecology work.

records.caution: Venomous species. Observe from a safe distance and never prompt handling or close-up scale counts for casual users.

records.sourceTitle: The Reptile Database, Ophiophagus salvatana, Das et al. 2024

facts.value: A Luzon king cobra identified as a distinct Philippine species in a 2024 revision of the Ophiophagus hannah complex.
The taxonomic diagnosis includes adult band pattern differences and more angular pale body bands in juveniles than in some congeners.
Older 'king cobra' records may refer to a broader species complex and cannot be automatically mapped to this taxon.

records.caution: Highly venomous. No handling, approach, capture or intrusive photography. Retain an uncertain Ophiophagus identification unless a qualified review supports species attribution.

records.sourceTitle: IUCN Red List, Rusa alfredi, 2016 global assessment

facts.value: The IUCN's 2016 global assessment lists the Philippine spotted deer as Endangered, with a decreasing trend. This is not an undated current estimate.
The assessment lists forest, shrubland and grassland environments and identifies hunting and habitat degradation as threats.
A Philippine endemic deer of the Western Visayas; the regional reference must not be used as a survey-site occurrence.

records.caution: Camera detections need diagnostic pelage and body views, camera identity, deployment nights and avoidance of duplicated individuals.

records.sourceTitle: Bat Conservation International, Giant Golden-crowned Flying Fox

facts.value: A very large fruit bat with golden fur on the head, contrasting with its darker body; identification depends on visible characters and size context.
The species feeds heavily on fig fruit in mature lowland forests and roosts in trees, sometimes with Pteropus bats.
The Bat Conservation International account notes forest loss, hunting and roost disturbance as central concerns.

records.caution: Do not confuse this large flying fox with Pteropus species from silhouettes alone. Record roost flights without disturbing colonies.

records.sourceTitle: Journal of Threatened Taxa, Rediscovery of the Dinagat Bushy-tailed Cloud Rat

facts.value: An endemic cloud rat documented from Dinagat Island. Published rediscovery work follows the original 1975 specimen.
The journal describes this group of rodents as arboreal, leaf-feeding and nocturnal; confirmed species-specific behaviors remain sparse.
The rediscovery study distinguishes actual encounters from unconfirmed local reports.

records.caution: The known records are sparse. Do not assume an arboreal rodent sighting elsewhere is this species or publish exact sensitive locations.

records.sourceTitle: American Society of Mammalogists Mammal Diversity Database, Crateromys heaneyi

facts.value: A cloud rat endemic to Panay and associated with lowland primary and secondary evergreen rainforest in the source summary.
The database records the original description by Gonzales and Kennedy in 1996 and accepts the species in the genus Crateromys.
The MDD account displays Endangered as its cited global status, not a DENR national assessment.

records.caution: Specialist photographs or specimens are needed to distinguish similar cloud rats. Do not treat captive behavior studies as verified wild behavior.

records.sourceTitle: IUCN Red List, Sus oliveri, 2016 global assessment

facts.value: Oliver's warty pig is endemic to Mindoro; records occur mainly near forested parts of its central and northwestern mountain ranges in the cited assessment.
Habitat degradation, hunting and hybridization with domestic pigs are named concerns.
The 2016 IUCN assessment lists Vulnerable and flags the account as needing a future update.

records.caution: The species' exact habitat preference and behavior are poorly known. Older specialist reports use a different IUCN assessment category; preserve dates and sources.

records.sourceTitle: Field Museum, Philippine bare-backed fruit bat natural-history account

facts.value: The membrane of the wings attaches unusually close to the back's midline, producing the bare-backed appearance despite underlying fur.
Historical accounts describe colonies in coastal or lowland limestone caves on Negros and evening travel to fruiting forest habitats.
The Field Museum describes seasonal reproductive colonies at known historic cave roosts. These records do not show breeding at other sites.

records.caution: Never disturb cave maternity roosts. Photographing a bare-backed bat should not involve entering roost chambers solely for identification.

records.sourceTitle: Animal Diversity Web, Little golden-mantled flying fox

facts.value: A small flying fox recorded from several Philippine faunal regions; records on individual islands still require confirmation.
The account describes tropical lowland forest as a principal environment.
Identify the species using proportion and facial/fur characters against related Pteropus taxa; a small golden-colored bat alone is not diagnostic.

records.caution: Flight-only sightings of small fruit bats are rarely sufficient for species-level records. Include photo context and estimate uncertainty.
